sentences.text: The genus name combines Greek words meaning “terrible lizard”.

The holotype includes an incomplete but connected skeleton preserving most of the skull and much of the neck, torso vertebrae, belly ribs, both upper arms, the pelvis and the majority of the right hind limb.
Digital modelling indicates the skull could reach about 90 cm in length.
More than six-tenths of the skull length is taken up by the snout, which stays at a fairly uniform height from front to rear.
The upper jaw of the holotype bears 13 teeth, while a referred specimen shows 15 teeth.
The lower jaw of the holotype contains 16 teeth, a count comparable to that of related albertosaurines.
Stuart Plotkin uncovered the holotype in 2010 within the upper Oldman Formation of Alberta, Canada.
The find occurred near the Provincial Dinosaur Park and was aided by a University of Alberta team during 2010–2011.
The specimen is catalogued as UALVP 52981 and resides in the university’s Vertebrate Paleontology Laboratory.
Mark J. Powers and colleagues formally described Tromerosaurus solumons in 2026, naming the holotype as the type specimen.
Additional material, including two isolated maxillae from unknown sites—one from a mature individual and another from a small juvenile—has been tentatively assigned to the species.
Two other fossils, TMP 1994.012.0602 and TMP 1995.005.0001, were referred based on shared anatomy with the holotype.
Parsimony analyses consistently recover Tromerosaurus as the most basal member of Albertosaurinae, the subfamily that also contains Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus.
The same researchers noted that the animal displays a mixture of features seen in both albertosaurines and early tyrannosaurines.
Tromerosaurus lived in what is now Canada during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Bayesian phylogenetic methods placed the taxon as the earliest branch of Tyrannosaurinae, making it the sister group to Albertosaurinae, which conflicts with the parsimony outcome.
These opposing results underscore the mosaic nature of its anatomy, combining traits of two major tyrannosaurid lineages.
